newsitem.title: UK: Brazil economy outlook not so bad - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Brazil economy outlook not so bad - analysts.

text.p: Two London-based analysts on Thursday said prospects for the Brazilian economy were brighter than many commentators have predicted.

"We are more optimistic than most about the immediate fiscal outlook and regard the widening current account (deficit) as a natural corollary of successful structural reforms rather than the mask of disgrace," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said in a research note.
A large portion of Brazil's deficit reflects new foreign investment, it added.
The real is also not as overvalued as some investors think, and Brazil is far more capable of sustaining a current account deficit than Argrntina or Mexico, the bank said.

"Provided the current account deficit can be contained below Brazil's long-run growth potential, as a percentage of GDP, which we believe it can...(it) should not be a source of major instability in the foreign exchange market," the bank said.
But a further round of fiscal reform is clearly needed, though the growth of public sector debt should slow next year.

"The fiscal outlook for 1997 is for some improvement, giving the government the breathing space to introduce essential longer-term measures, not least the advancement of the privatisation programme," the bank said.

There is a fairly benign outlook for fixed-income investors, but government reluctance to let foreign exchange reserves fall too far and so reduce the scope for a Brady bond buy-back could hurt Brazilian Brady bond prices..
Stockbrokers Stephen Rose and Partners said the next three months would be critical.

"All eyes...will be on the federal government and Congress to see what it delivers. We believe that it will deliver more than the current rather jaundiced view expects and that the market will be given a kick start," it said.

The imptues for the stock market rise will be evidence that President Fernando Henrique Cardoso is likely to stay in power for another six years, that constitutional reform is gathering momentum, privatisation is going ahead and that economic growth is picking up.
"This should entice the foreigners back into the market, provided world markets do not keel over and persuade all equity buyers to put up the shutters," it added.
